source: codeconnect-oct-2026/devoxx-slot/cutting-edge.md (28/10): seven ideas, each claim checked against the transcripts there
standfirst: Seven ideas that were genuinely new. Some of the sharpest were in talks almost nobody had saved.
tableStakes: Most AI talks taught good practice, not the edge: short rules files, checks the agent can't edit, sandboxes, a second model reviewing.

ideas.title: Loops replace prompts
ideas.line: You design the checker and when to stop, not the prompt.

talks.fact: Named it loop engineering. The agent that writes the code never grades its own work in the same conversation.
An agent-built feature passed 51 of 52 behaviour checks, yet most of 13 architecture rules failed.
Agents chase the goal you wrote, not the one you meant, so the checker must be out of their reach.
Same model, different harness, different score. A bash-only harness beat Claude Code.

ideas.title: Define correct, and agents build whole systems
ideas.line: A spec plus tests the agent can't change turns months of work into days.

talks.fact: Agents built a certified Jakarta EE runtime, about 300k lines, against the official test kit. Once, they cheated it.
223 PRs in 11 days for about $2,000 in tokens. By hand he estimated more than six months.
A Parquet parser built with Claude Code, its output checked against two existing Parquet readers.
Write a test kit from your spec; the prompt becomes "comply with the new version of the test kit".

ideas.title: Distil, then step out
ideas.line: Let the model find a path that works, then freeze that path into plain code.

talks.fact: A free agent gave a different credit verdict each run. Paths proven in evals became fixed code; the LLM only writes the summary.
Ask the AI for a script that draws the diagram, not the diagram. A script costs nothing to rerun and can't hallucinate.
Log triage: about $3,000 a ticket on a top model, $1.26 with plain parsing and a cheap model as fallback.
A better prompt plus a summing tool beat a model five to ten times as expensive.

ideas.title: Review gets new instruments
ideas.line: Humans review architecture, plans and assumptions, not 5,000-line PRs.

talks.fact: Groma.md: an always-current map of the system, with architecture diffs next to the code diffs.
No human reviews before a fresh AI has. The agent rates its confidence in each assumption, so you know where to look.
The IDE splits in three: review tools, managers for fleets of agents, and language smarts for agents.
Review a 300-line plan instead of a 5,000-line PR.

ideas.title: One agent became a fleet
ideas.line: The hard part now is running many agents at once, safely apart.

talks.fact: The genuinely new problem: many agents changing one codebase at the same time.
Each agent runs in its own microVM, and the real API key never enters it.
Idle agents are snapshotted and resumed on any node in under half a second.
A virtual IT department of role agents burned tokens on chatter. One orchestrator with small tasks worked.

ideas.title: Context is a supply chain
ideas.line: Skills and rules are now versioned packages, and a way in for attackers.

talks.fact: A Koog skill lifted success to 92%, because Koog is too new to be in the model's training data.
Agent definitions and skills moved to one shared repo after personal setups caused team friction.
MCP's July 2026 spec adds Skills over MCP: skills get distributed like packages.
Hidden instructions in skills and unpinned installs: he compares it to npm around 2015.

ideas.title: Frontier models are now attackers
ideas.line: AI finds vulnerabilities faster than most teams patch them.

talks.fact: Claude Mythos was the first model to finish the UK AISI's 32-step attack range (3 of 10 tries).
Spring: over 200 CVEs since April, against about 177 in the previous 13 to 14 years.
Firefox found 22 vulnerabilities in two weeks with Claude Code. curl ended its bug bounty.
